title: Situation Summary: Venezuela: Earthquakes - Jun 2026
content:
• Since the 24 June earthquakes (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5) in north-central Venezuela, there have been 1,463 aftershocks reported.  
• Official figures report 5,398 deaths, 16,740 injured, and 17,907 people displaced due to loss of homes.  
• The United Nations and partners are scaling up multisectoral response efforts, targeting 1.3 million affected people over six months with a US$299 million funding appeal.  
• WFP has provided food assistance to over 120,000 people through diverse modalities including hot meals, ready-to-eat rations, food baskets, and electronic vouchers, and is supporting logistics for relief supply distribution.  
• Funding secured for the response is approximately one third of the US$80 million WFP requires to sustain and expand assistance for 500,000 people over three months.  

Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two strong earthquakes and numerous aftershocks, causing significant casualties and displacement. The government is managing transitional camps while the UN and partners continue to scale up aid delivery. Funding gaps remain a critical challenge to fully meet the urgent food, shelter, health, and protection needs of the affected population.

title: Situation Summary: Afghanistan
content:
• Fuel prices in Afghanistan have surged sharply due to supply shortages from Russia and export bans, with diesel prices rising 3.1% in one week and remaining 19% above last year’s levels, driving inflation in food and non-food items.  
• Food prices continue to increase, with wheat and flour prices 8–14% higher than last year, rice prices up 27–34%, and cooking oil rising by 4.6% in one week; vegetables like potatoes and tomatoes remain significantly more expensive year-on-year.  
• Non-food inflation is also notable, with fertilizer prices up 19–51% compared to last year, while livestock prices are slightly lower than last year, and unskilled labour availability has declined by 17%, reducing household income opportunities.  
• Heavy flash floods on 20 July in eastern Afghanistan, particularly in Parun City, Nuristan Province, caused at least 23 deaths, 125 injuries, and destroyed or damaged 92 houses, along with critical infrastructure such as health clinics, roads, bridges, and water supply networks.  
• UNICEF and partners responded rapidly, delivering emergency health services to over 600 people within 24 hours, but the floods have severely disrupted livelihoods and access to safe drinking water in the affected areas.  

Afghanistan is facing compounded humanitarian challenges from rising inflation driven by fuel price shocks and supply constraints, alongside acute disaster impacts from recent flash floods in the east. These dynamics are exacerbating food insecurity, limiting income opportunities, and damaging critical infrastructure, increasing the need for sustained emergency response and support to vulnerable populations.

title: Situation Summary: Venezuela: Earthquakes - Jun 2026
content:
• Two powerful earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, followed by 1,463 aftershocks, causing widespread destruction and a national emergency declaration.
• Official figures report at least 5,398 deaths, 16,740 injuries, and 17,907 people displaced due to destroyed or severely damaged homes; over 23,500 people are currently sheltering in 107 transitional camps.
• Humanitarian needs are critical in food security, healthcare, safe water, sanitation, psychosocial support, and shelter; over 120,000 people have received food assistance from WFP, while Project HOPE operates eight mobile medical units providing primary and maternal healthcare.
• Infrastructure damage includes 2,501 assets affected, with 856 buildings damaged or collapsed, disruption to electricity, water, telecommunications, transport, and healthcare services; debris removal is minimal, with only 1% cleared in La Guaira.
• A US$299 million addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan was launched to address the needs of 1.3 million people over six months, raising total funding requirements for Venezuela’s humanitarian response to US$931 million.

The earthquakes severely impacted Venezuela’s strategic northern coastal region, including La Guaira, a critical hub for transport, trade, and connectivity to the capital Caracas. The disaster has compounded existing vulnerabilities, with economic inflation rising sharply and limited humanitarian presence in some affected states. The response is transitioning from search and rescue to recovery and reconstruction, with ongoing challenges in debris clearance, infrastructure repair, and addressing the mental health and protection needs of affected populations.

title: Situation Summary: Afghanistan
content:
• Heavy rainfall and flash floods from 20–21 July have severely affected multiple provinces in Afghanistan, with Parun City in Nuristan Province the hardest hit, reporting 23 deaths, 5 missing, 125 injured, and 92 families eligible for humanitarian assistance. Significant damage occurred to homes, infrastructure, markets, water supply, agricultural land, and livestock.

• Flooding also impacted Paktika, Paktia, Ghazni, Maidan Wardak, Kapisa, Nangarhar, and Laghman provinces, causing casualties, destruction of houses, loss of livestock, and damage to roads and irrigation systems. Assessments and response efforts are ongoing in these areas.

• Humanitarian response includes emergency health services, shelter support (tents, winter kits, blankets), food assistance, water and sanitation interventions, protection services including psychosocial support and gender-based violence prevention, and plans for cash assistance to affected families.

• Concurrently, Afghanistan faces rising inflation driven by a sharp increase in fuel prices, particularly diesel and petrol, due to supply shortages from Russia and limited alternatives. This has led to broad-based increases in food prices (wheat, flour, rice, cooking oil, vegetables) and non-food items (fertilizers), while labour market opportunities remain limited.

• The fuel price shock and inflationary pressures are exacerbating the cost of transportation and supply chains, impacting household purchasing power and food security, particularly in flood-affected and vulnerable communities.

The recent floods have compounded existing economic challenges in Afghanistan, where rising fuel and food prices are already straining household incomes and livelihoods. The humanitarian response is focused on immediate relief and early recovery, but ongoing inflation and supply constraints may hinder recovery efforts and increase vulnerability in affected populations.

title: Situation Summary: Bangladesh
content:
• Heavy monsoon rains, flash floods, and landslides have affected approximately 1.28 million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, with 436,000 estimated to require humanitarian assistance and 59 deaths reported as of 22 July 2026.  
• Extensive damage has been reported to housing (74,479 houses damaged or destroyed), water points (29,076), and latrines (36,550), severely impacting access to safe water and sanitation in 42 upazilas.  
• Livelihoods and food security are severely affected, with 27,007 hectares of cropland damaged and over 266,000 livestock impacted, resulting in combined losses estimated at US$17.3 million in livestock and fisheries sectors.  
• Bangladesh Red Crescent Society has reached over 23,000 households with dry food, provided safe drinking water and purification supplies, supported more than 1,500 people with mobile medical teams, and evacuated over 22,000 people.  
• Planned response activities include distribution of food packages to 7,500 households, multipurpose cash assistance to 2,570 households, scaling up rescue and WASH services, mobilising shelter materials, and deploying additional medical and water treatment teams.  

The ongoing monsoon season continues to pose risks, with forecasts of heavy rainfall and landslide advisories in key affected districts. Government, humanitarian agencies, and partners are actively scaling up response efforts to address urgent needs in food security, health, WASH, shelter, and protection while conducting assessments and recovery planning.

title: Situation Summary: Sudan
content:
• In June 2026, WFP reached a record 3.7 million people in Sudan with food assistance, including 1 million in areas at Risk of Famine, and 1.4 million received cash-based transfers, the highest monthly figure since the conflict began.  
• WFP faces critical funding shortages, with food stocks expected to run out by September and cash-based transfer funding projected to end in August, risking the loss of support for millions.  
• On 20 July 2026, drone strikes in Al Rahad, North Kordofan, hit a health centre and a market area, causing at least 6 child casualties (2 killed, 6 injured) and 4 adult deaths, with over 20 others injured.  
• A drone strike on 19 July killed 13 civilians in Al Musallamiya village, and another alleged strike on 21 July targeted a girls' primary school in Al Hugeina village, injuring one teacher; these incidents are under verification.  

The humanitarian situation in Sudan remains dire, with escalating violence including drone attacks on civilian areas and critical shortages in food assistance due to funding gaps. The combination of conflict-related casualties and potential famine risk underscores the urgent need for increased humanitarian support and protection measures.

title: Situation Summary: Ukraine
content:
• In 2025, humanitarian assistance in Ukraine focused on house repairs, construction materials, window replacements, and Rapid Thermal Kits, reaching over 2,150 households through five assessments conducted in early to mid-2026.

• During the 2025-2026 winter, Russian forces launched at least 423 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing widespread electricity outages that severely affected millions, especially vulnerable groups in multistory buildings amid temperatures below -20°C.

• The highest winter-related risks for 2026-2027 are concentrated in north-east and eastern oblasts (Kharkivska, Sumska, Donetska, Kyivska), where harsh weather overlaps with active conflict, displacement, and damaged utilities; large urban centres like Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro also face significant vulnerability due to infrastructure disruptions.

• Lack of basic services such as electricity, water, and heating was a major factor driving displacement abroad during winter 2025-2026, with about 75% of people leaving Ukraine citing these reasons; restoration of electricity is a key consideration for potential returnees.

The ongoing conflict and repeated targeting of critical energy infrastructure have compounded humanitarian needs in Ukraine, especially during harsh winters. The disruption of essential utilities not only affects daily living conditions but also influences displacement patterns and return decisions, highlighting the urgent need for durable solutions to restore and protect infrastructure and support vulnerable populations.

title: Situation Summary: occupied Palestinian territory
content:
• WFP is providing monthly cash assistance to 100,000 households in the occupied Palestinian territory from July, with full transfers to the most vulnerable and reduced transfers for others, to extend aid through late November amid funding shortfalls.  
• Without new funding, WFP plans to reduce in-kind food assistance from October, currently provided at a 75 percent ration, which would result in fewer people receiving aid.  
• Recent IPC analysis indicates some improvements in food security and child nutrition in Gaza, driven mainly by humanitarian interventions rather than recovery of livelihoods or local systems, making progress fragile.  
• Shelter Cluster partners reached 36,210 households in Gaza with shelter and non-food items (NFIs) in June, distributing tarpaulins, kitchen sets, bedding, tents, clothing vouchers, and sealing kits to address urgent needs.  
• Critical shortages of essential household items remain, with supplies sufficient for fewer than 15,300 households; urgent facilitation of material entry is needed to sustain shelter responses, especially during the summer.  
• Emergency repairs were completed on 1,837 makeshift shelters and 1,025 partially damaged homes in June, with cumulative totals of 2,696 upgraded shelters and approximately 1,299 rehabilitated homes.  
• Distribution of solar-powered lamps to 7,200 households in displacement sites is ongoing, but pipeline constraints and delays in receiving materials such as solar lights, timber, ropes, and tools are limiting shelter response capacity.

The humanitarian situation in the occupied Palestinian territory remains precarious, with significant needs in food security, shelter, and essential household items. While some improvements in nutrition and food security have been recorded, these are dependent on continued humanitarian assistance rather than sustainable recovery. Funding shortages and supply chain constraints threaten to reduce aid coverage and slow shelter rehabilitation efforts, underscoring the urgent need for increased funding and facilitation of aid deliveries.

title: Guatemala: Earthquake - DREF Final Report (MDRGT026)
content:
Description of the Event

What happened, where and when?

On 8 July 2025, the central region of Guatemala was shaken by a series of earthquakes with epicenters located in the departments of Sacatepéquez and Escuintla. These seismic events aected several localities in those departments, as well as municipalities within the department of Guatemala.

According to ocial reports, the rst earthquake occurred at 3:11 p.m. with a magnitude of 5.2, triggering a seismic sequence that reached its peak at 3:41 p.m. with a second tremor measuring magnitude 5.6. Both events had their epicenter in Santa María de Jesús, located in the department of Sacatepéquez.

Information from the National Institute of Seismology, Volcanology, Meteorology and Hydrology (INSIVUMEH) indicates that by 15 July— exactly one week after the initial event—a total of 1,062 earthquakes had been recorded, 36 of which were reported as felt by the population. The seismic activity was concentrated primarily along the border area between Sacatepéquez, Escuintla, and Guatemala departments.

INSIVUMEH further reported that the focal mechanism analysis of the seismic sequence was conducted using FMNEAR software, conrming that the earthquakes were related to ruptures in normal and strike-slip fault systems. The solutions obtained were considered high quality, with condence levels above 70%, providing a high degree of precision to the applied seismic model and allowing for an accurate understanding of the magnitude and characteristics of the events.

On the same day, 8 July, the National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction (CONRED) announced the declaration of a nationwide Institutional Orange Alert. This measure was taken in response to the recent seismic activity as well as the presence of multiple concurrent threats posing risks to the population. As part of the alert, response plans were activated at local, municipal, and departmental levels, and the public was urged to follow the authorities' guidance and act responsibly.

On 9 July 2025, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance (MSPAS) issued a statement announcing the activation of an Institutional Red Alert for the health service networks in the departments of Sacatepéquez, Escuintla, and Guatemala. This decision was made within the framework of the "Institutional Operational Protocol for Geological Threats" with the goal of anticipating potential impacts on health infrastructure and ensuring the continuity of essential health services, even in the event of aftershocks or additional seismic events.

On 12 July, the Municipal Coordinator for Disaster Reduction (COMRED) declared a Municipal Institutional Red Alert in the municipality of Santa María de Jesús due to the emergency caused by seismic activity.

Following this declaration, the emergency response became the responsibility of CONRED at the departmental level in Sacatepéquez. In the departments of Escuintla and Guatemala, the response was coordinated by CONRED at the national level.

By the end of 2025, seismic activity associated with the July earthquake sequence had decreased compared with the initial emergency period. However, seismic monitoring continued throughout the year, as Guatemala remained exposed to recurrent seismic activity due to its geological conditions.

According to INSIVUMEH, a total of 11,811 seismic events were recorded nationwide in 2025, of which 397 were reported as felt by the population. The highest levels of seismic activity were recorded in July and August, with 2,533 and 2,246 seismic events respectively. July also reported the highest number of felt earthquakes, with 145 events, followed by August with 75.

Although seismic events continued to be monitored until the end of the year, no additional major humanitarian impacts directly linked to the July earthquake sequence were identied in the available information by the end of the operation.

title: WFP Sudan Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In June, WFP reached 3.7 million people, the highest monthly number in 2026, driven by WFP’s strong logistical and procurement capacity, ability to access hard-to-reach areas, close coordination with partners and government counterparts, and the scale-up of both in-kind food assistance and cash-based transfers (CBT).
  • Of all the people reached, 1 million received assistance in areas classified as at Risk of Famine (RoF).
  • WFP reached 1.4 million people through CBT in June, also the highest monthly reach achieved since the onset of the conflict.
  • WFP is facing severe funding constraints. Without additional resources, WFP's food stocks are expected to be exhausted by September, while funding for lifesaving CBT assistance is projected to run out in August, leaving millions of vulnerable people without support.

title: WFP Zambia Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP and partners supported livelihood interventions that reached 1,000 refugee households and 200 host-community households in the Mantapala Refugee Settlement, strengthening climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, and seed systems to support long-term resilience and recovery.
  • Preparations commenced for a South-South learning exchange with Namibia to share Zambia’s experience in school feeding programme design, procurement systems, and coordination mechanisms, strengthening regional collaboration and positioning Zambia as a leader in Home-Grown School Meals programming.
  • WFP’s Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) monitoring indicated a favourable food security outlook in June, supported by the strong 2025/26 harvest, improved food availability, declining inflation, and a reduction in the national cost of the basic food basket.

title: WFP Ethiopia Country Brief July 2026
content:
• WFP reached 1.8 million food insecure people with 10,700 metric tons of food and USD 4.5 million in cash assistance across all activities.
  • WFP continued to provide fuel to partners through On-Demand Services (ODS) to mitigate fuel supply constraints and address earlier delays.
  • WFP will provide food assistance to new South Sudan arrivals in the Gambella Region.
  • WFP supported 40,500 households across seven regions through resilience and livelihood activities, including climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, market systems and nutrition-sensitive livelihoods.

title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report, 23 July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #93, 24 July 2026 (Reporting period: 1-15 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Funding shortfalls are impacting WFP’s ability to meet significant humanitarian needs. From July, WFP will provide monthly cash assistance to 100,000 households through a revised, vulnerability-based approach, maintaining full transfers to the most vulnerable households and reduced transfers for others, which will help extend available cash assistance through late November.
  • Additional funding is urgently needed to prevent further reductions in food assistance. Without new contributions, in-kind assistance, which is already being provided at a 75 percent ration, will be reduced from October, with fewer people receiving reduced rations.
  • Newly released IPC analysis shows improvements in food security and child nutrition across Gaza, however progress remains fragile, with the improvements driven largely by expanded humanitarian food, nutrition and health interventions rather than a recovery of livelihoods, local food systems or essential services.

title: Ukraine Situation: Moldova - Operational Update (June 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

As of June 2026, 141,528 refugees from Ukraine are in the Republic of Moldova, many of whom continue to face challenges in meeting basic needs and achieving self-reliance. While the Temporary Protection (TP) holders retain access to primary healthcare services and family doctors, access to specialized health care and essential medicines has deteriorated. The latest Participatory Assessment found that 20 per cent of refugee households identify healthcare as an urgent need, while 31 per cent require more information on available medical services. These challenges are largely driven by the closure or scale-down of humanitarian health and cash assistance programmes and the lack of corresponding government funding to absorb these services into national systems, leaving many vulnerable refugees to cover consultation, treatment and medication costs out of pocket.

Economic inclusion remains a significant challenge. Participatory Assessment findings show that only 20 per cent of surveyed refugees are employed and 1 per cent are self-employed, despite a strong willingness to work. Language barriers, skills mismatch, caregiving responsibilities and limited access to suitable jobs continue to constrain labour market participation, particularly among women, older people, and persons with disabilities, highlighting the need for targeted employment support measures.

title: WFP Sao Tome and Principe Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS
• Commissioning began across 14 schools in Sao Tome that received solar panels and kitchen equipment, including electric pressure cookers and refrigerators.
• In May, partners and WFP leadership visited program areas, including Principe Island, to support the Green Infrastructure for Education Project handover and assess the impact of current interventions and future needs.
• WFP, as the Accredited Entity for the Green Climate Fund Project Preparation Facility, led high-level consultations with the Government and stakeholders.
• Sao Tome and Principe will organize the Presidential and legislative elections in July and September respectively. Campaigns for the Presidential elections started in June which resulted in reduced field activities.

title: Ivory Coast Cholera - DREF Final Report (MDRCI018)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
01-08-2025
What happened, where and when?

On 5 June 2025, health authorities confirmed a cholera outbreak in the village of Vridi Ako (also referred to in some early alerts as Ako Brakré), located in the Port-Bouët Vridi health district of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The area, home to approximately 19,800 inhabitants—mainly fishing communities and migrants—has long been vulnerable to waterborne diseases due to poor sanitation, limited access to safe drinking water, and recurrent flooding.

While the first confirmed cases were reported in early June in Vridi Ako, retrospective epidemiological investigations indicated that alertsignals and suspected cases had already emerged in late May, explaining the discrepancy in reported start dates across different reportsand surveillance updates.

Following confirmation of the outbreak in Vridi Ako, the situation evolved rapidly from a localized outbreak into a multi-district epidemic. Within days, additional cases were reported beyond the initial epicentre, first spreading to nearby peri-urban and coastal areas, and subsequently extending to five additional health districts: Yopougon Est, Jacqueville, Sassandra, Fresco, and San Pedro. This marked a clear transition from a concentrated outbreak in Port-Bouët Vridi to a wider geographic spread affecting both urban and coastal periurban settings.

The epidemiological curve showed two distinct phases of transmission intensity. The first peak occurred in June, concentrated in Vridi Ako, reflecting rapid local transmission driven by environmental contamination and high population mobility. A second and more geographically dispersed peak followed in July, associated with the emergence of new transmission hotspots in Yopougon Est and Sassandra, indicating secondary spread and establishment of additional foci outside the initial epicentre. A particularly high-risk cluster was also identified in a detention centre in Abidjan, where overcrowding and inadequate sanitation conditions accelerated transmission dynamics.

This escalation from a single-community outbreak to a multi-district epidemic required a corresponding scale-up of the response. As an auxiliary to public authorities, the Red Cross Society of Côte d’Ivoire initially supported rapid needs and situation assessments during the first alerts in late May and early June, leveraging pre-positioned volunteers in Vridi Ako. As the outbreak expanded geographically and intensified during the July peak, the National Society scaled up operations across affected districts, reinforcing its WASH activities, health interventions, and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) to address both containment in the original hotspot and prevention of further spread in newly affected areas.

Despite continued transmission over several months, the outbreak gradually declined after the second peak. On 1 December 2025, the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene officially declared the end of the outbreak across all six affected health districts. In total, 556 cases and 24 deaths were reported over the course of the epidemic.

By the end of the operation, no new cholera cases were being reported, and the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene officially declared the end of the outbreak on 1 December 2025. Transmission had been interrupted across all six affected health districts.

However, important vulnerabilities remained in the affected communities, which continue to face overcrowding, recurrent flooding, inadequate sanitation, and limited access to safe water. Communities also expressed continued socio-economic needs and requested sustained support beyond the emergency phase.

While health facilities resumed normal operations, many still faced shortages of medical supplies and equipment. To support preparedness, first-contact health centres in all affected districts were provided by CRCI with essential medical and hygiene supplies, including chlorine and soap during this operation to ensure sustainability of interventions beyond the outbreak.

As part of the exit strategy, trained teams in the Abidjan detention centre remained operational and continued implementing disinfection activities using equipment provided by CRCI and the ICRC.

In addition, recognizing the socio-economic impact of the epidemic, CRCI mobilized complementary funding to provide cash assistance to vulnerable households in Vridi Ako in February 2026, ahead of the Lent and Ramadan periods.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 304: Week 3 – July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Fuel Price Shock and Exchange Rate Dynamics:

A sharp spike in fuel prices is emerging as a primary driver of inflationary pressure, with the cost of transportation cascading into other food and non-food items. This increase is directly impacting supply chains and delivery costs, driven by rising diesel prices. The main catalysts are deepening supply shortages from Russia, exacerbated by the export ban and damage to critical refining infrastructure. Over the past two weeks, limited alternative supplies from Central Asian countries, Iran, and Iraq have contributed to the price surge. Beyond diesel, consumers in parts of the country are reporting shortage of gas used for cooking appliances, with prices rising sharply. Similarly, petrol prices have surged from around AFN 66 to AFN 82 per litre. Concurrently, while the Afghani remained broadly stable at AFN 65.9/USD, it has exhibited an upward trend in recent weeks, depreciating by 2.5% compared to the third week of June. However, it remains 4% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, which continues to partially moderate imported inflation.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed broad-based upward pressure during the third week of July, with rising transportation costs increasingly contributing to price movements across several commodities.

• Wheat and Flour: All wheat categories rose by around 1% week-on-week, remaining elevated compared to last year—wheat grain (+14%), high-price flour (+8%), and low-price flour (+12%)—reflecting sustained production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Both rice categories edged up modestly and remained substantially above last year's levels, with high-price rice 27% higher and low-price rice 34% higher, standing significantly above their three-year average levels.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil surged by 4.6%, the sharpest weekly increase among staples, while sugar rose modestly (+0.5%) and pulses and salt remained largely stable. Year-on-year, prices of cooking oil (+8%), sugar (+10%), and salt (+8%) remains elevated, whereas pulses show a 14% decline.

• Vegetables: Potato prices continued to climb (+2.2%), while tomato and onion saw marginal increases. Year-on-year, tomato and potato remained significantly elevated by 35% and 55%, respectively, while onion prices eased by 9%, reflecting improved seasonal availability.
Non-Food Items:

• Fuel: Diesel prices continued their sharp upward trajectory, increasing by 3.1% during the week, mainly due to higher international oil prices and continued supply constraints from Russia. Compared to last year and the three-year average, diesel prices remained 19% and 21% higher, respectively.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices rose during the week, with DAP increasing by 1.7% and Urea by 1.1%. However, compared to last year, DAP and Urea remained considerably higher by 19% and 51%, respectively. Improved seed and animal feed prices stayed below last year and the three-year average, reflecting weak consumer demand.

• Livestock: The price of a one-year-old live female sheep increased marginally by 0.4% during the week but remained 6% below last year's level and 2% below the three-year average, contributing to weaker pastoralist ToT.

• Labour Market: Daily wage unskilled labour availability remains limited at 2.0 days/week which is 17% lower than last year and the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on household income opportunities

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 103 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 18 Jul 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #30 (23 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 30
Earthquakes in Venezuela
23 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

Note

Starting with this edition, the report will be published on a weekly basis. The next edition will be released on 30 July. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: 345W Preparedness and Response.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 2, 01-22 July 2026
content:
Situation update

  • Cholera outbreak continues to spread in Cameroon’s Far North Region, with 585 reported cases and 19 deaths as of 22 July 2026 across height affected health districts. The outbreak remains active, with a case fatality rate of 3.25% and 172 cases under treatment.
  • Children and vulnerable populations remain disproportionately affected, with a median age of 24 years. Ongoing cross-border movements and limited access to safe water and sanitation continue to increase the risk of further transmission.
  • UNICEF has activated a multisectoral response in support of government-led efforts, covering Health, WASH, SBC/AAP, Child Protection, Youth Engagement, and coordination. Additional flexible funding is urgently required to rapidly scale up life-saving interventions, strengthen preparedness, and prevent further transmission.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2, 01 Jan-30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Cameroon continued to face a complex humanitarian situation during the first half of 2026, driven by protracted conflict in the North-West and South-West, insecurity in the Far North, the cholera outbreak and climate-related shocks. These overlapping crises continued to expose millions of children and vulnerable families.
  • UNICEF and partners sustained an integrated humanitarian response, expanding access to health, nutrition, education, child protection and WASH services while strengthening community engagement, accountability to affected populations, social cohesion, and outbreak preparedness despite persistent insecurity and humanitarian access constraints.
  • Humanitarian funding increased to US$4.9 million, reducing the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children funding gap from US$52.3 million (97 per cent) to US$48.9 million (91 per cent). Despite this progress, critical funding shortages continue to constrain the scale-up of life-saving assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

During the first half of 2026, Cameroon continued to face multiple and overlapping humanitarian crises driven by protracted conflict, population displacement, public health emergencies, climate-related shocks and recurrent localized disasters. The crises in the North- West and South-West (NWSW) regions and insecurity in the Lake Chad Basin (LCB) continued to affect children, women and vulnerable communities, limiting access to essential services, disrupting livelihoods and increasing protection risks.

The humanitarian situation further deteriorated during the second quarter with the emergence of a cholera outbreak in the Far North Region, affecting the health districts of Fotokol, Mada, Makary,
Kolofata., Maroua III and Kousseri. The outbreak occurred within a broader regional context, with neighbouring Chad and Nigeria simultaneously responding to cholera outbreaks, increasing the risk of cross-border transmission in this highly mobile border area.

Limited access to safe water and sanitation, poor hygiene conditions, seasonal flooding, population movements and weak health systems continued to fuel transmission and complicate response efforts. At the same time, Cameroon continued responding to Mpox and yellow fever outbreaks, further stretching already fragile health systems.

Across crisis-affected regions, children remained exposed to heightened risks of acute malnutrition, communicable diseases, violence, family separation, psychosocial distress and prolonged disruption of education. In the Far North, insecurity, recurrent attacks, climate shocks, food insecurity and cross-border population movements continued to undermine livelihoods and access to health, nutrition, WASH, education and child protection services. On July 2026, new displacement alert reported that approximately 100 households (600 people) had settled in a spontaneous emergency site in Andilbine 2, Makary, following repeated incursions by nonstate armed groups in the localities of Nage and Kimbelo, Hile Alifa.

Fires affecting internally displaced communities in Kolofata further increased humanitarian needs during the reporting period. In the NWSW regions, persistent insecurity continued to restrict humanitarian access and the delivery of essential services, particularly in hard-to-reach communities.

Despite continued humanitarian response efforts, needs consistently outpaced available resources. Persistent insecurity, access constraints, weak infrastructure, recurrent displacement and critical funding shortfalls continued to limit the scale and continuity of assistance. Additional flexible funding is urgently required to sustain integrated life-saving interventions, contain disease outbreaks including cholera, strengthen preparedness and cross-border coordination, and ensure that vulnerable children and their families receive timely, equitable and resilient support across Cameroon.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Flash Update #1 (Eastern Region Flash Floods), 23 July 2026
content:
Situation Overview

• On 20 July, heavy rainfall triggered flash floods across three provinces in eastern Afghanistan. The most severe impact was reported in Parun City, Nuristan Province, where extensive flooding caused deaths, injuries, significant damages with disruption of services to the affected communities.

• Preliminary reports1 indicate 23 fatalities and 125 injuries, with additional individuals still missing. The floods destroyed and damaged 92 houses, while also impacting a health clinic, markets, and disrupting local livelihoods.

• Critical infrastructure and services sustained damages, including bridges, road sections, flood protection walls, agricultural land and damaged water supply networks, disrupting access to safe drinking water.

• Within 24 hours, UNICEF with partners were on the ground, providing immediate lifesaving emergency health services to cover over 600 people including children.

title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Flash Update No. 1 (Mpox Outbreak Response), 4–20 July 2026
content:
Situation Update

The Ministry of Public Health officially declared Guinea-Bissau’s first mpox outbreak on 4 July 2026. To date, three laboratory-confirmed cases have been reported: a 27-year-old female in Bissau (Cuntum) confirmed on 23 June; a 40-year-old male in Bissau (Bairro Militar); and a 19-year-old female in Safim (Biombo Region) confirmed on 13 July. A total of 26 contacts—9 in Bissau and 17 in Safim—are under active follow-up. No deaths have been reported.

The delay between symptom onset and isolation, alongside the lack of clear epidemiological links between cases, suggests undetected transmission is likely ongoing. While health authorities have not officially commented on the specific strain, the West African Clade II virus is the anticipated driver given its regional endemicity across West Africa. Finalizing the 42-day action plan remains a critical window of opportunity for early containment.

title: WFP Response to the Ebola Outbreak - External Situation Report (23 July 2026)
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

• The Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak continues to spread in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) affecting 47 health zones across five provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, and Haut-Uele. While Ituri accounts for 90 percent of confirmed cases, recent spread to Tshopo (Kisangani) and Haut-Uélé increases the risk of wider transmission as Kisangani is a major transport hub. The outbreak is now spreading faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and has become the third-largest Ebola outbreak on record.

• In DRC, the outbreak is unfolding in a complex humanitarian environment, marked by conflict, large-scale displacement, limited access to basic services, including food, nutrition, clean water, shelter, health care, and protection, and an ongoing health workers strike.

• Community unrest continues to constrain surveillance and response activities. In July, WFP experienced two security incidents, including an attack that affected UNHAS operations in Niania, and community unrest in the Bule IDP site. WFP continues to engage local leaders and communities.

• In Uganda, no new cases have been reported since 21 June 2026. A 42-day enhanced surveillance period has started before the outbreak can be declared over in the country. National authorities in Uganda and the DRC, in collaboration with WHO and partners, continue to implement extensive preparedness and response measures.

title: UNHCR Somalia Protection and Solutions Monitoring Network (PSMN) Quarterly Report | April – June (Q2) 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Somalia experienced three markedly different displacement patterns across Q2 2024, Q2 2025 and Q2 2026.
Total recorded displacement stood at 148,167 movements in Q2 2024, declined by 49 per cent to 75,843 in Q2
2025, and then rose sharply to 216,979 in Q2 2026. The 2026 total was therefore almost three times the Q2
2025 level and 46 per cent higher than Q2 2024.

The change was not only quantitative. The principal causes and geographical distribution of displacement also
shifted substantially:

  • Q2 2024 was dominated by widespread flooding, particularly in Belet Weyne and Afmadow.
  • Q2 2025 remained flood-dominated, but displacement was heavily concentrated in Jowhar and Balcad.
  • Q2 2026 became a compound conflict-drought crisis, with conflict accounting for 53 per cent and
    drought for 35 per cent of all movements.

Conflict and drought together generated 191,648 movements in Q2 2026, equivalent to 88 per cent of the national total. Flood displacement declined significantly, but remained locally severe in Belet Weyne, Jowhar and Banadir.

The geographical pattern also broadened. In Q2 2025, the three most affected districts accounted for 61 per cent of national displacement. In Q2 2026, this fell to 47 per cent, indicating that several major emergencies were occurring simultaneously across southern, central and northern Somalia.

Banadir became the leading displacement hub, recording 65,944 movements in Q2 2026, followed by Buuhoodle, Diinsoor, Laas Caanood, Bossaso, Galdogob, Jalalaqsi and Gaalkacyo.

Overall, the findings point to a transition from episodic, hazard-specific displacement to a more geographically dispersed and multi-causal crisis. Conflict, drought, livelihood erosion, market disruption, weakened coping capacity and urban concentration increasingly reinforce one another.
