title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #14 (17 to 19 July 2026)
content:
The fourteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 17 to 19 July.

Highlights

Between 17 and 19 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities across La Guaira, Falcón and Carabobo, through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and information management.

To date, IOM has reached 8,210 unique individuals through 14,959 instances of assistance and services, primarily in shelter and site coordination, health, WASH and protection.

During the reporting period, IOM completed 229 household needs surveys in three transitory camps, supported the renewal of 19 identity documents at Tanaguarena Golf Course and advanced improvements at Mare Abajo II, including the installation of ten showers for women.

IOM Activities

IOM continues to support five transitory camps in La Guaira and affected communities in other states through shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and mental health, protection, registration, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM ensured essential services for 316 families. At Mare Abajo II, it advanced the installation of family cubicles, internal partitions, bunk beds and electrical connections. At Tanaguarena Golf Course, IOM registered 155 tents and coordinated the installation of additional units.

At César Nieves Stadium, 11,000 litres of water were supplied and 12 cubic metres of waste were collected. At Playa Grande, 24,000 litres of water were distributed and 1.1 tonnes of waste were removed. At Mare Abajo II, 30,000 litres of water were delivered to 125 households in the camp and nearby communities, showers for women were completed and drainage works continued.

At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, 18 mobile health and MHPSS sessions have been conducted, providing a cumulative total of 1,519 consultations. Medical consultations, medicine distribution, psychosocial support and sexual and reproductive health services also continued across the other camps.

IOM updated population records at César Nieves Stadium, Playa Grande and Tanaguarena Golf Course, and completed 229 household surveys to assess the population’s needs, mobility dynamics and intentions.

In the area of protection, IOM maintained specialized screening, legal counselling and referrals to specialized services. It also supported identity document renewal, child protection activities and efforts to prevent trafficking in persons, violence against women, and sexual exploitation and abuse.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening the management and improvement of transitory camps, including the installation of tents, family cubicles, toilets, showers, lighting, electrical connections, and water and drainage systems.

IOM will also maintain comprehensive health and MHPSS services, protection screening and referrals, multisectoral assessments and mobility monitoring. In addition, it will advance assessment missions and distributions of essential items in Carabobo and Falcón, while strengthening coordination and information management to identify available services, operational actors and remaining gaps.

title: UNICEF State of Palestine Situation Update and Humanitarian Response (Mid-Year Analysis of the Response to the Needs of Children), 17 July 2026
content:
Gaza Strip Situation Update

  • Humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip remain dire, with most of the population – 1.9 out of 2.1 million people – displaced and exposed to ongoing health and environmental risks.
  • Access restrictions and operational constraints continue to disrupt humanitarian delivery, with only 280 out of 633 UNICEF aid trucks (44 per cent) from Egypt able to offload during May and June 2026.
  • Essential services remain critically limited: access to healthcare, water, sanitation, and protection services continue to be disrupted by destruction or damage to critical civilian infrastructure, and movement restrictions.
  • Severe restrictions on the entry of fuel, spare parts, and essential materials – including engine oil required to operate generators – are driving system failures across health and WASH services.
  • In the WASH sector, conditions remain critical. An estimated 82 per cent of families are water insecure, and up to 70 per cent cannot access 6 litres per person per day – far below minimum emergency standards – placing children at direct risk of dehydration and waterborne disease.
  • Nearly 90 per cent of water and sanitation infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed. Limited latrine access, unsafe disposal practices, and disrupted sludge management compromise infection prevention and control, increase the risk of healthcare-related infections, the growing presence of rats and other disease vectors, and contribute to widespread environmental contamination.

title: UNFPA Flash Update #2 on the situation in El Obeid, North Kordofan, Sudan (3 - 19 July 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in North Kordofan continues to deteriorate. Between 1 and 19 July, 21 drone-related incidents were recorded, resulting in civilian casualties, damage to critical infrastructure, and further disruptions to the already limited access to essential services.

Access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services and protection from and response to gender-based violence (GBV) remain severely limited in North Kordofan due to the security situation, damaged and overstretched health facilities and service delivery points, and shortages of qualified health personnel, essential medicines, and medical supplies. In addition, water shortages, inadequate sanitation, and deteriorating living conditions are increasing health risks for women and girls, particularly pregnant and lactating women.

An additional US $1.83 million is urgently required for UNFPA to sustain and scale up preparedness and response activities for SRH and GBV interventions for conflict-affected women and girls in North Kordofan and White Nile states.

title: UNHCR Romania: Ukraine Refugee Situation Update, Weekly Update #205, 20 July 2026
content:
Highlight

20 July 2026 More than four years after the start of the full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians remain displaced, with 3.8 million internally displaced within Ukraine and nearly 5.8 million refugees worldwide, including over 5.2 million in Europe. In Romania, more than 212,000 refugees remain under temporary protection. In this context of protracted displacement and continued uncertainty, understanding refugees' intentions and the factors shaping their decisions is essential for informing policies and durable solutions. UNHCR's seventh Lives on Hold report presents findings from 4,375 refugee household interviews conducted across Europe between December 2025 and January 2026. Among refugees surveyed in Romania, 46 per cent said they would be likely to return to Ukraine if the war ended, increasing to 75 per cent if the war ended and Ukraine regained control over all temporarily occupied territories, while 9 per cent remained undecided and 17 per cent said they would be unlikely to return under either scenario. Building on previous research on return intentions, this latest edition explores how refugees' plans and aspirations may differ depending on how the war evolves and eventually ends, recognizing that future scenarios will significantly influence decisions about returning to Ukraine.

Response and Advocacy

During the past week, UNHCR’s partner, the Romanian National Council for Refugees (CNRR), delivered legal counselling and protection support to 133 Ukrainian refugees across Romania, focusing on access to social assistance, education, healthcare and housing. Through individual case management, CNRR supported refugees in overcoming administrative barriers affecting access to essential services and social benefits. The organization also continued to engage with relevant authorities to clarify procedures, resolve documentation issues and strengthen referral pathways. CNRR assisted newly arrived and vulnerable refugees in accessing emergency accommodation and healthcare, including by facilitating referrals to municipal social services and supporting registration with family doctors. Protection counselling was provided to survivors of gender-based violence, refugees with serious medical needs to access treatment, and helped families navigate higher education admission procedures and other administrative requirements to promote longer-term inclusion and self-reliance. Since the beginning of 2026, UNHCR and its partners have provided protection counselling and legal support to 4,962 refugees.

UNHCR continues to support refugees through community-based activities at its Community Centre for refugees at RomExpo, in Bucharest, providing opportunities to strengthen skills, foster social connections and support integration into the host community. On 15 July, a session of the Romanian Speaking Club, supported by a community volunteer and UNHCR colleagues, brought together refugees in an informal and welcoming environment to practise Romanian through interactive discussions and speaking exercises. The session explored summer-related vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation and everyday conversations, including travel situations. The Romanian Speaking Club helps refugees build confidence in using Romanian in daily life, while promoting social inclusion through language practice, community engagement and meaningful interaction with native speakers.

title: Empowering Displaced People through EU-Funded Acted’s Community Resource Centre (CRC) in Yemen
content:
In Yemen, humanitarian conditions are expected to further deteriorate in 2026, with projections indicating that 22.3 million individuals will require humanitarian assistance—an increase from the 19.5 million reported in the previous year. Since 2015, Al Dhale’e, a frontline governorate, has been facing repeated displacement into remote and insecure areas, which has caused further access constraints, delayed assistance, and limited access to services and information.

Inadequate Access to Services and Support

Hind*, a 48-year-old mother of seven and a former teacher, fled her home in Hudaydah in 2020 due to the war and now lives in Eastern Sahda Camp in Al Dhale’e. Like many others, her family faced daily challenges, including finding food, securing shelter, and searching for assistance.

Hind describing lack of access to information before the establishment of the CRC, Al Dhalee district, Al Dhale'e governorate, April 2026

The main challenge was the distance. We had to travel far to reach assistance, and that was difficult for families like ours.

Hind

Marwan*, a 38-year-old farmer and father of five, was also displaced because of the war in 2020. He now lives in Al-Hussein District, Al Dhale’e Governorate. He says it was difficult for displaced families to find reliable information on available assistance and reach the right organisations.

We struggled to get information about the assistance available. We also faced problems when trying to submit complaints or reach the related organisations.

Marwan

Acted’s Community Resource Center (CRC)

Acted established the CRC in Al Dhale’e in July 2025 to ensure displaced families and host communities can access timely support in one place. Through the centre, Hind and Marwan found a safe and supportive space where they could express their needs, receive guidance, access information, share feedback and complaints, and be connected to available services.

The CRC forms part of the Area-Based Site Management (ABSM) approach, implemented by Acted with funding from the European Union through the Yemen Displacement Response (YDR) Consortium, enabling displacement-affected communities to access information, services, and support through a centralised and community-focused platform.

Community Resource Center (CRC) in Al Ajab Village, Al Dhalee district, Al Dhale’e governorate, April 2026

Hind says her first visit to the centre gave her a better understanding of the support available.

I went to the centre because I needed help as a displaced person. When I arrived, I was warmly welcomed, and the staff listened carefully to my needs.

Hind

Marwan had a similar experience.He says, “To be frank, the feelings I had were indescribable. During that time, I was living in a state of complete stress.” When he arrived, the staff received him well. “They welcomed me and listened attentively,” he says. “They asked about my situation and explained what could be done.”

EU-Funded Support That Made a Difference

After assessing their needs and referring them to appropriate services, the CRC helped Hind and Marwan access humanitarian assistance that improved their living conditions. “The centre helped connect us with immediate support.” says Hind.

I received humanitarian emergency assistance, including the provision of shelter, hygiene kits, and cash assistance.

Marwan

Marwan (on the left) giving feedback at the CRC in Al Ajab Village, Al Dhalee district, Al Dhale’e governorate, April 2026

“Thank you for all the joy you have brought into our lives, and even more; indeed, the one who guides others towards good is rewarded just as much as the doer is,” Hind concludes.

Marwan shares the same appreciation. “When I received the news of the support, the heavy burden of worry and stress was lifted off my shoulders.”

Acted empowers people like Hind and Marwan by helping them identify where to turn and what steps to take to access available support. In many cases, the CRC acts as a hub that provides awareness sessions and referrals to other organisations that could provide direct support.

CRC Impact At-A-Glance

  • Acted received assistance requests from 1,913 individuals (937 male, 976 female) through the CRCs.
  • Acted managed 974 complaints (635 male, 339 female), ensuring transparent and responsive feedback.
  • Acted held coordination meetings and provided various training and awareness sessions (Code of Conduct, CRC services, Community Mobiliser training, and more) to 927 individuals (703 male, 224 female).

Code of Conduct awareness workshop at the CRC in AlAjab Village, Al Dhalee district, Al Dhale’e governorate, April 2026

As part of the project “Improving living conditions and supporting durable solutions for displacement-affected communities across Yemen” launched in 2023, funded by the European Union through its Humanitarian Aid Operations and delivered in partnership with the YDR Consortium, Acted CRCs across Al Dhale’e, Aden and Marib have assisted 3,815 individuals (2,940 internally displaced persons and 875 host community members). This has enabled displaced families to access clear information, referrals, and guidance.

*Names of beneficiaries have been changed to protect their privacy.

The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel, which began in October 2023 and spiked in September 2024, entered a new phase in early
2026. Although a November 2024 ceasefire was put in place, persistent daily violations and Israel's continued occupation of five
positions in southern Lebanon blocked reconstruction and the return of displaced residents. The truce officially collapsed on March 2,
2026, following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, which triggered retaliatory Hezbollah rocket and drone attacks, subsequent heavy Israeli
bombardments, expanded ground operations, and widespread evacuation orders across southern Lebanon and Beirut's southern
suburbs.

fragile November 2024 truce collapsed following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. Hezbollah's retaliatory rocket and drone attacks
prompted a massive Israeli response, shifting from "limited" incursions into an intensified ground campaign and heavy bombardments
that triggered widespread evacuation orders across southern Lebanon and Beirut's southern suburbs. Amid this escalation, UNIFIL has
faced severe operational constraints in its final mandate year; with peacekeepers killed, patrols targeted, and infrastructure damaged,
the mission's ability to monitor and document violations along the Blue Line has been deeply compromised.

targeted, and monitoring infrastructure damaged, undermining the mission’s ability to document violations along the Blue Line. Israeli
military operations intensified throughout March and May 2026, evolving from “limited” operations into a broader ground campaign
extending deeper into southern Lebanon.
Following the massive military escalation that began in early 2026, Israel has targeted thousands of sites across Lebanon. While a
breakthrough in early June led to a US - brokered ceasefire agreement outlining "pilot zones" for Lebanese army control, the diplomatic
framework remains highly fragile. Hezbollah officially rejected the truce, demanding a full Israeli military withdrawal, while ongoing
localized violence including an IDF strike on Beirut's southern suburbs and a major Hezbollah rocket barrage on June 7 continues to
threaten a total collapse of the ceasefire, leaving over 1 million civilians displaced amid climbing casualties.
Between April and June 2026, Lebanon's humanitarian crisis deepened severely. The Ministry of Public Health reported that casualties
since March climbed to over 3,613 killed and 11,072 injured, with women, children, and the elderly making up more than a third of the
civilian toll. Continuous airstrikes flattened neighborhoods, schools, and nearly 200 healthcare facilities across Southern Lebanon, the
Bekaa Valley, and Beirut's southern suburbs, keeping 1.2 million people displaced and completely overwhelming shelters in cities like
Tyre and Saida.

title: Sudan Crisis Situation Analysis (Period: 15/06/26 - 21/06/26)
content:
Sudan is facing one of the world’s largest humanitarian and displacement crises as the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces
(SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, enters its fourth year in 2026. The conflict has triggered
widespread civilian suffering, economic collapse, mass displacement, and severe regional instability, with humanitarian conditions
continuing to deteriorate across much of the country.
An estimated 19.5 million people are currently experiencing acute food insecurity, making Sudan the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Famine conditions have been confirmed in el-Fasher (North Darfur) and Kadugli (South Kordofan), while multiple areas across Darfur
and Kordofan remain at high risk of famine amid ongoing conflict, siege tactics, market disruption, and severe restrictions on
humanitarian access. Children continue to bear a disproportionate burden of the crisis, with millions exposed to acute malnutrition,
disease outbreaks, and heightened mortality risks.
Fatality estimates remain highly contested due to limited access, communication blackouts, and verification constraints. The Armed
Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded nearly 30,000 reported deaths by late 2024, while independent analyses and
international media estimates suggest the true death toll may exceed 150,000 people. Civilians continue to face widespread violence,
including indiscriminate shelling, aerial bombardments, drone attacks, and ethnically targeted violence, particularly in Darfur and
parts of Kordofan.
Sudan’s health system remains severely degraded, especially in active conflict zones where many facilities are non-operational or
functioning only partially. Although the nationwide cholera outbreak that spread across all 18 states between 2024 and early 2026 was
declared contained in March 2026, underlying conditions—including mass displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and poor
sanitation—continue to create a high risk of renewed outbreaks and other communicable diseases.
Displacement continues at an unprecedented scale. More than 14 million people have been displaced since the start of the conflict,
including approximately 9 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) and over 4 million refugees in neighboring countries, making
Sudan the world’s largest displacement crisis. At the same time, limited and fragile returns to parts of Khartoum and Al Jazirah have
been reported since early 2026 following shifting frontlines, though returnees face widespread destruction, insecurity, and lack of basic
services and livelihoods.
Militarily, the conflict has continued to fragment since late 2025, with intensified fighting in Darfur and Kordofan driving further civilian
displacement and humanitarian access constraints. The RSF maintains significant influence across much of Darfur and continues
offensive operations in Kordofan, while the SAF retains control over key eastern and northern urban centers. The growing use of drones,
aerial strikes, and long-range attacks has increasingly impacted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, markets, and
displacement sites, further compounding humanitarian needs.

Ethnic violence and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) continue to escalate, particularly in Darfur. Human rights organizations
and monitoring networks have documented widespread abuses, including conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement,
arbitrary detention, and targeted attacks on ethnic communities. Despite sustained international pressure, including sanctions

title: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Heavy Rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #3 (2026-07-20)
content:
Description

Within minutes on the morning of 17 July, flash floods carrying large volumes of water, mud and debris swept across National Highway 32, inundating homes and posing an immediate threat to lives and property. The floods claimed five lives, while three people remain missing beneath mud and debris. Eight people were injured, and dozens of households were evacuated from high-risk areas as an emergency precaution.

The floods affected 53 houses, including 20 houses that were completely washed away. Approximately 300 hectares of rice fields, crops and aquaculture areas were buried or swept away. Several transport routes, irrigation facilities, schools and power systems were also damaged.

Although floodwaters have now receded, widespread destruction remains, with many affected households continuing to face the impacts of the disaster.

Immediately following the disaster, local authorities activated emergency response measures. Provincial and commune-level Civil Defence Command Committees were deployed to affected areas to coordinate search and rescue operations, restrict access to dangerous roads, and evacuate people from areas at risk of landslides. The province mobilised nearly 1,000 personnel, along with multiple vehicles and equipment, to support disaster response and recovery efforts.

The flash floods were triggered by persistent heavy to very heavy rainfall across the northern mountainous region, where cumulative rainfall over the past three days generally ranged from 150–300 mm. The highest accumulations were recorded at Chế Tạo (Lào Cai) with 474 mm, Nậm Păm (Sơn La) with 350 mm, Nà Tấu (Điện Biên) with 277 mm, and Pa Thắng (Lai Châu) with 250 mm.

Further rainfall is expected to hamper response and recovery efforts. On 20 July, moderate to heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast across the northern mountainous region and Quảng Ninh Province, with widespread rainfall of 20–50 mm and isolated areas expected to receive more than 100 mm. Short-duration intense rainfall exceeding 70 mm within three hours is possible. Other parts of northern Viet Nam are forecast to experience scattered showers and thunderstorms, with rainfall of 10–20 mm and isolated areas receiving more than 50 mm.

According to reports from Lào Cai, Lai Châu, Điện Biên and Sơn La provinces, heavy rainfall, floods, inundation, flash floods and landslides from 15–19 July 2026 caused the following impacts:

Human impact: Five people were killed, three remain missing, and 10 people were injured, all reported in Lai Châu Province.

Housing: A total of 36 houses collapsed (Lai Châu: 24; Lào Cai: 1; Sơn La: 11); 391 houses were damaged (Lai Châu: 35; Lào Cai: 305; Điện Biên: 27; Sơn La: 24); 140 houses required emergency relocation (Lào Cai: 71; Lai Châu: 26; Điện Biên: 3; Sơn La: 40); and 194 houses were affected by flooding and landslides (Lai Châu: 51; Lào Cai: 65; Điện Biên: 20; Sơn La: 58).

Agriculture: A total of 707 hectares of rice and crops were affected (Lào Cai: 76.45 ha; Lai Châu: 409.51 ha; Điện Biên: 27.24 ha; Sơn La: 193.80 ha).

Livestock: Approximately 250 livestock and poultry were killed or washed away.

Transport infrastructure: Landslides affected multiple sections of roads, including national highways (QL4H, QL12, QL32 and QL279) and provincial roads in Lai Châu (ĐT127, ĐT128, ĐT129, ĐT133, ĐT133B, ĐT134, ĐT135, ĐT138 and ĐT138C); QL279, QL32 and ĐT175B in Lào Cai; 32 locations along ĐT109 in Sơn La; and QL12, QL279 and ĐT143 in Điện Biên, as well as various inter-village and inter-commune roads.

As of the latest update, traffic remains disrupted at Km139+300 on National Highway 279. Vehicles are currently being diverted through the new bypass section of QL279 in Lào Cai.

The total estimated economic loss is approximately VND 362.46 billion (Lai Châu: VND 190 billion; Lào Cai: VND 45.16 billion; Sơn La: VND 125 billion; Điện Biên: VND 2.3 billion).

In addition to search and rescue efforts for missing persons, response forces have been supporting local authorities in evacuating people and their belongings from hazardous areas, setting up temporary shelters, transporting essential supplies, and assisting affected communities to stabilise their living conditions amid the ongoing complex flood situation. On the morning of 19 July, a delegation from the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment visited and inspected areas affected by the recent floods in Mường Than. The delegation met with affected communities and response personnel involved in disaster recovery efforts. Deputy Minister acknowledged the proactive efforts of local authorities and response forces in mobilising resources for search, rescue and relief operations. He also requested local authorities to continue prioritising support for families who lost loved ones, accelerate the search for missing persons, ensure affected households have access to basic living conditions, and urgently restore damaged transport infrastructure, electricity and water supply. Authorities were also requested to conduct thorough assessments of affected areas and develop relocation plans for households whose homes were destroyed.

title: Sudan Crisis Situation Analysis (Period: 22/06/26 - 28/06/26)
content:
Sudan is facing one of the world’s largest humanitarian and displacement crises as the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, enters its fourth year in 2026. The conflict has triggered
widespread civilian suffering, economic collapse, mass displacement, and severe regional instability, with humanitarian conditions
continuing to deteriorate across much of the country.
An estimated 19.5 million people are currently experiencing acute food insecurity, making Sudan the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Famine conditions have been confirmed in el-Fasher (North Darfur) and Kadugli (South Kordofan), while multiple areas across Darfur
and Kordofan remain at high risk of famine amid ongoing conflict, siege tactics, market disruption, and severe restrictions on
humanitarian access. Children continue to bear a disproportionate burden of the crisis, with millions exposed to acute malnutrition,
disease outbreaks, and heightened mortality risks.
Fatality estimates remain highly contested due to limited access, communication blackouts, and verification constraints. The Armed
Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded nearly 30,000 reported deaths by late 2024, while independent analyses and
international media estimates suggest the true death toll may exceed 150,000 people. Civilians continue to face widespread violence,
including indiscriminate shelling, aerial bombardments, drone attacks, and ethnically targeted violence, particularly in Darfur and
parts of Kordofan.
Sudan’s health system remains severely degraded, especially in active conflict zones where many facilities are non-operational or
functioning only partially. Although the nationwide cholera outbreak that spread across all 18 states between 2024 and early 2026 was
declared contained in March 2026, underlying conditions—including mass displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and poor
sanitation—continue to create a high risk of renewed outbreaks and other communicable diseases.
Displacement continues at an unprecedented scale. More than 14 million people have been displaced since the start of the conflict,
including approximately 9 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) and over 4 million refugees in neighboring countries, making
Sudan the world’s largest displacement crisis. At the same time, limited and fragile returns to parts of Khartoum and Al Jazirah have
been reported since early 2026 following shifting frontlines, though returnees face widespread destruction, insecurity, and lack of basic
services and livelihoods.
Militarily, the conflict has continued to fragment since late 2025, with intensified fighting in Darfur and Kordofan driving further civilian
displacement and humanitarian access constraints. The RSF maintains significant influence across much of Darfur and continues
offensive operations in Kordofan, while the SAF retains control over key eastern and northern urban centers. The growing use of drones,
aerial strikes, and long-range attacks has increasingly impacted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, markets, and
displacement sites, further compounding humanitarian needs.

Ethnic violence and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) continue to escalate, particularly in Darfur. Human rights organizations
and monitoring networks have documented widespread abuses, including conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement,
arbitrary detention, and targeted attacks on ethnic communities. Despite sustained international pressure, including sanctions
imposed by the United States and United Kingdom on RSF leaders and affiliated networks, diplomatic and mediation efforts have yet to
achieve a durable ceasefire or political settlement.
The conflict is also generating increasing regional spillover, with large refugee flows, cross-border insecurity, and growing pressure on
already overstretched humanitarian systems in neighboring countries. Humanitarian operations inside Sudan remain critically
underfunded, with the World Food Programme warning in 2026 that severe funding gaps are threatening emergency food pipelines,
ration levels, and the continuity of lifesaving assistance.
As of mid-2026, Sudan remains one of the world’s most severe and complex humanitarian emergencies, characterized by prolonged
armed conflict, fragmented territorial control, mass displacement, and shrinking humanitarian space. Without urgent improvements in
humanitarian access, sustained financing, and renewed diplomatic engagement, the crisis is likely to deepen further, with serious
implications for civilian populations and broader regional stability.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territories (oPt) Crisis Situation Analysis (Period: 15/06/26 - 21/06/26)
content:
The Occupied Palestinian Territory is facing a severe humanitarian crisis, with both Gaza and the West Bank experiencing unprecedented levels of violence and deprivation. In Gaza, following the collapse of a brief pause in hostilities in March 2025, Israeli forces resumed intensive bombardment while maintaining a complete blockade that has now entered its eighth week, preventing all humanitarian aid and commercial supplies from entering. This has left Gaza's 2.2 million residents facing starvation as food stocks deplete, bakeries cease operations due to lack of flour and fuel, and nearly 90% of the population remains displaced with critical infrastructure almost entirely destroyed. A new U.S.-backed peace plan led to a pause in hostilities agreement coming into effect on 10 October 2025, raising cautious hopes for increased humanitarian access and a potential reduction in hostilities after months of relentless violence. However, despite the pause in hostilities, sporadic violations, limited aid entry, and continued displacement highlight the fragility of the pause in hostilities and the deep humanitarian strain that persists across Gaza.

Meanwhile, the West Bank has seen a dramatic escalation in military operations, particularly since the launch of "Operation Iron Wall" in January 2025, which has resulted in mass displacement of Palestinians and widespread destruction across refugee camps. Israeli forces have displaced approximately 40,000 people, with officials stating that residents will not be allowed to return for at least a year, while expanded checkpoints and military presence severely restrict movement between Palestinian cities.

International organisations and UN bodies have expressed increasing concern about systematic violations of international humanitarian law in the West Bank, including accelerating settlement expansion, land reclassification and forced displacement that multiple observers warn are driving de facto annexation dynamics. These concerns have intensified following the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion on the illegality of the prolonged occupation and the Israeli authorities' security cabinet decisions of 8 February 2026 expanding civil and administrative control over West Bank land and governance.

title: Africa CDC Epidemic Intelligence Weekly Report, July 2026
crisis: Central African Republic: Cholera Outbreak - Jun 2026
content:
Welcome to our Epidemic Intelligence Weekly Report, your trusted source for real-time updates on priority events of concern on the continent. The narrative brought to you focuses on three main areas: the epidemiological situation, event assessment (risk assessment and geoscope) and public health interventions by the affected Member State, partners, and Africa CDC. Every week we highlight events reported to Africa CDC that rank from moderate to very high risk as per the Africa CDC risk assessment tool.

Geographic Focus: Reports could either focus on events affecting single country or multiple countries.

Inclusion criteria: While Africa CDC continues to track all public health events on the continent, this report highlights only moderate to very high-risk events (with new updates in the reporting week).

Events: We focus on a range of health threats, ranging from emerging infectious diseases to endemic conditions, and natural disasters. We follow a one-health multisectoral approach highlighting events across all relevant sectors: animal, environmental and human.

This Event-Based Surveillance Weekly Report is your compass for navigating Africa’s public health landscape. We empower you with the latest information and insights, for informed decisions and effective interventions to attain a healthy and prosperous Africa.

Stay informed. Stay vigilant. Stay safe.

title: WFP Kenya Country Brief July 2026
content:
• WFP reached 1.2 million crisis-affected Kenyans and refugees in June through food assistance and resilience building interventions.
  • There is a growing likelihood of an El Niño event based on the latest forecasts. WFP and partners are working on readiness and anticipatory actions.
  • WFP is contributing to evidence generation, including through the Standardized Expanded Nutrition Survey (SENS), the national Long Rains Assessment, and food security analyses, to ensure that interventions are targeted, effective and respond to evolving needs.
  • To support the drought response, WFP procured approximately 1,300 metric tons of food commodities from smallholder farmers and specialized nutritious foods from local producers, injecting USD 3.2 million into the economy.

title: WFP Somalia External Sitrep July 2026
content:
• Catastrophic Levels of Food Insecurity (IPC5) risk in Bay and Bakool: FEWSNET assesses a plausible risk of IPC Phase 5 in Bay–Bakool Agropastoral zones between June and September 2026 in the event of a second consecutive failed Gu harvest, and between October 2026 and January 2027 under an extreme, widespread Deyr flooding scenario comparable to 1997 or 2019.
  • Nutrition Famine threshold crossed in Buur Hakaba District: Buur Hakaba has reached IPC Acute Malnutrition Phase 5, with a GAM rate of 37.1 percent, surpassing the famine threshold and signalling a credible risk of area-level Famine between June and September 2026.
  • Three Compounding Shocks. Rising food prices driven by consecutive poor harvests and broader supply-chain disruptions linked to the Middle East crisis, an emerging El Niño raising the risk of flash flooding in low-lying areas of Bay and Bakool during the Deyr season, and ongoing disease outbreaks are compounding vulnerabilities across Buur Hakaba, Bakool, Gedo, and Hiiraan.
  • Humanitarian assistance is contracting as need rises. Food security assistance nationally is down by 51 percent from March to April 2026; Nutrition sites in Buur Hakaba fell from 16 to three since 2024; and only 34 of 111 villages remain fully accessible.
  • The response is severely underfunded. the 2026 HNRP is only around 15 percent funded, in Buur Hakaba USD 3.2 million of the USD 4.62 million requirement is unfunded.
  • The window closes with the Deyr rains. 2017 and 2022 show that early, funded response averts famine. Anticipatory action ahead of October to December 2026 is the most cost-effective option left this year.
  • Displacement on the rise: internal and cross borders displacements are increasing, with 197,500 new displacements expected in the Q3 of 2026 (IOM, June 2026) flooding and drought as the main driver.

title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report 19 July 2026
content:
Situation Update
• Twenty-five days after the twin earthquakes of 24 June, authorities report 5,208 deaths and 16,740 injuries. Following search and rescue operations, national authorities have shifted the efforts toward relocating displaced populations to transitional camps.
• According to authorities, 107 transitional camps have been established, with 23,828 people currently accommodated. As part of the UN-coordinated response, WFP is supporting three camps with two hot meals daily.
• WFP Acting Executive Director Carl Skau spoke with Venezuela's Acting President, Delcy Rodríguez, and reaffirmed the organization's commitment to continuing its support to authorities and humanitarian partners in meeting immediate food needs and assisting affected families in their recovery.

title: Situation Report: June 2026 WHO Cox’s Bazar: Rohingya Emergency Response
content: 1. Overview In June 2026, WHO supported disease surveillance, outbreak response, and essential health services for approximately 1.7 million refugees and host community members, while advancing measles control, dengue preparedness, routine immunization, and emergency readiness. However, critical funding gaps continue to threaten key public health functions and service delivery. 2. Coordination and Leadership WHO, as Health Sector lead, continued to coordinate the health response for Rohingya refugees and host communities, supporting strategic planning, partner alignment, and evidence-based decision-making. Key updates:  Analysis of the 2026 Joint Response Plan (JRP) funding status identified major gaps in critical health interventions. WHO faces a 64% funding gap in its Health Sector coordination and leadership functions. From September 2026, this gap will reduce WHO's capacity to coordinate partners and lead the Health Sector response. Funding shortfalls will also affect infectious disease surveillance, outbreak detection, and response activities (P1) from July 2026. This will weaken early warning, health-risk monitoring, data analysis, and operational decision-making in a densely populated and vulnerable setting.  The WHO-led Health Sector and UNICEF-led Nutrition Sector completed a joint assessment of all 42 Primary Health Centres (PHCs) to inform a phased integrated of health and nutrition service delivery. The assessment provides the evidence base to determine facility readiness for integration, establish realistic implementation timelines, and support coordinated planning between both sectors.  Regular coordination mechanisms continued to strengthen partner alignment on public health priorities, preparedness, operational planning, and response activities, supporting coordinated health service delivery across all camps.  The Health Sector sustained strategic engagement with donors, government counterparts, and partners to advocate for additional resources, address critical funding gaps, and maintain continuity of life-saving health services.  Health Sector information products (4W, HeRAMS, Early Warning, Alert and Response System (EWARS) reports, and epidemiological updates) continued to support planning, monitoring, and resource allocation: https://rohingyaresponse.org/sectors/coxs-bazar/health/

title: Eritrea Project Highlights: Emergency support to vulnerable pastoralists and agropastoralists in response to lumpy skin disease outbreaks in the Gash Barka, Debub, Anseba and Maekel regions
content:
Objective

To strengthen the resilience of pastoralist and agropastoralist livelihoods by improving the control of lumpy skin disease (LSD) through targeted vaccination, enhanced surveillance and community awareness in high-risk areas. Activities implemented • Procured 500 000 doses of LSD vaccine and implemented targeted vaccination campaigns in hotspot and riverine areas. • Vaccinated approximately 530 000 cattle, representing more than 25 percent of the national livestock population. • Trained 60 field veterinarians and animal health officers on disease surveillance, biosafety, sample shipment, vaccination procedures and community awareness. • Distributed communication materials and conducted digital outreach activities to raise awareness and enhance community engagement. • Strengthened coordination with the Ministry of Agriculture and aligned interventions to ensure efficient vaccine deployment and response operations.

title: WFP Pacific Islands Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Following Typhoon Sinlaku in April 2026, which caused widespread damage to telecommunications infrastructure across Chuuk State in the Federated States of Micronesia, the WFP-led Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) deployed technical surge support to Chuuk State to help restore emergency telecommunications.

• The 35th Logistics Response Team (LRT) training, the first ever held in the Pacific, brought together humanitarian responders from across the globe in Suva, Fiji, to strengthen emergency logistics and inter-agency response capacity.

• The Government of Tonga launched the WFPsupported report Understanding the Experiences of Persons with Disabilities in Disasters and Emergencies in Tonga, advancing evidence-based and disability-inclusive disaster preparedness.

• The inaugural Humanitarian Warehouse Exchange programme was held in Brisbane in June to strengthen humanitarian warehousing and logistics capacities among Pacific partners.

title: WFP Chad Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• Chad hosts one of the largest displaced populations in the region, with over 2.25 million forcibly displaced people, including over 1.5 million refugees, over 492,000 returnees, and over 219,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs).
• Since April 2023, the conflict in Sudan has driven a massive influx into eastern Chad, with over 1.2 million people crossing the border, including 932,771 new arrivals from Sudan and 400,915 Chadian returnees.
• Cross-border arrivals into Chad are expected to continue in 2026. The majority have settled in the Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira, Sila, and Ennedi Est province.
• The continued influx of refugees and returnees from Sudan is placing additional pressure on already fragile local systems. These dynamics are increasing demands on food systems, basic services, and local resources, reinforcing the importance of sustained, coordinated humanitarian support alongside national efforts to promote stability and resilience.

title: UNHCR Returns to Syria Regional Update - (April - May 2026)
content:
REGIONAL TRENDS AND DEVELOPMENTS

As of 31 May 2026, an estimated 1.67 million Syrians had returned from neighbouring countries, alongside approximately 1.92 million internally displaced returnees, demonstrating continued interest in return despite significant reintegration challenges across Syria.

Return dynamics remained uneven across the region in May and April, reflecting differing protection environments and operational contexts. While returns from Lebanon and Türkiye continued at scale, movements from Egypt slowed due to operational and funding constraints affecting return support and school-year considerations. Returns from Iraq increased following the introduction of facilitated return procedures in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, while movements from Jordan remained relatively steady but below 2025 levels.

Return decisions continued to be driven by a combination of family reunification and perceived improvements in conditions in Syria, alongside hostilities and economic pressures in host countries.

Sustainable reintegration remains the principal challenge. Across Syria, returnees continue to face damaged housing, limited access to services and livelihoods, documentation obstacles, and broader recovery constraints, raising concerns about the sustainability of returns. UNHCR continues to support the Government's “no tent and no-camp” vision to advance return, reintegration and recovery efforts.

Findings from the Enhanced Regional Survey on Syrian Refugees' Perceptions and Intentions on Return to Syria (ERPIS), available here, confirm that while intentions to return have increased since the political transition, many refugees continue to monitor conditions closely and adopt a gradual, wait-and-see approach before making longer-term decisions.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 24 June - 07 July 2026
content:
For 10 years, attacks on health care have continued despite global commitments to protect patients and medical workers. Médecins du Monde's new report documents 223 attacks affecting its operations across conflict settings, revealing the devastating human toll and the growing erosion of humanitarian access. For a broader picture of the global pattern of violence against health care, see Insecurity Insight's report Still Under Attack: A Decade of Monitoring Attacks on Health Care after United Nations Security Council Resolution 2286, documenting the scale, patterns, and consequences of attacks on health care in conflict-affected settings worldwide. Among the report's key findings:

  • Over 17,500 attacks on health care were recorded between January 2016 and December 2025
  • Over 3,860 health workers were killed
  • Over 2,500 health workers were arrested or detained
  • Local health workers remain particularly vulnerable, accounting for more than 65% of health worker killings
  • The growing use of armed drones and explosive weapons is contributing to increasing damage to health facilities and health worker killings and injuries.

Based exclusively on Insecurity Insight’s data collection, it highlights how violence against health care is becoming normalised, with serious consequences for civilians, disease response and health systems. The report provides detailed analysis of perpetrators, methods of attack and emerging risks, including the growing role of new technologies in conflict environments. It also offers recommendations for governments, international organisations, humanitarian actors and the diplomatic community aimed at strengthening the protection of health care and improving accountability for violations.

title: WHO Afghanistan Emergency Situation Report No 65 (June 2026)
content:
Highlights

A significant investment in capacity building was made across Afghanistan, with 531 health workers trained in 14 different disciplines. WHO-supported health facilities delivered a high volume of essential services. This included 64 146 outpatient consultations, vaccinations for over 3000 children under five, and reaching 47 009 people in remote areas with health education and awareness materials. A 174% increase in suspected Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) cases compared to May, with 483 cases and 21 deaths reported in June alone.

title: IOM oPt: Shelter Overview | June 2026
content:
BACKGROUND

As the largest provider of shelter assistance in Gaza, IOM plays a central role in supporting displaced and conflict-affected households through a network of locally based partners. IOM cocoordinates the Shelter Cluster, strengthening the coherence and effectiveness of the shelter response across the sector, despite ongoing access constraints, shortages of shelter materials, widespread infrastructure damage, and prolonged displacement. By leveraging local expertise and available resources, IOM and its partners deliver adaptable, incremental shelter solutions that respond to rapidly changing humanitarian needs.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #26 (19 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 26
Earthquakes in Venezuela
19 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,388 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,208 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,388 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,208 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

title: Ivory Coast Floods 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRCI020)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
29-06-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 29 June 2026, the Autonomous District of Abidjan was hit by an episode of exceptionally intense rainfall occurring during the peak of the rainy season, which generally extends from May to July. These precipitations caused a rapid rise in water levels, resulting in widespread urban flooding, landslides, the collapse of houses, as well as major disruptions to socio-economic activities in several municipalities of the economic capital.

According to the Government of Côte d'Ivoire, 59 deaths have been recorded since the beginning of the rainy season, with the 28 and 29 June event representing the deadliest incident of the season to date. More than 3648 people affected, essentially in the municipalities of Attécoubé, Yopougon, Cocody and Songon were among the areas most severely affected. The most critical situation was recorded in the municipality of Attécoubé, specifically in the Mossikro neighbourhood, where a major landslide buried several houses. Search, rescue and victim recovery operations, led by the Military Fire Brigade Group (GSPM) with the support of national and local authorities, continued for several days to locate people who may have remained trapped under the debris.

These deadly incidents are the initial materialisation of above average rainfall forecasts for the current season. Indeed, forecasts indicated exceptionally high rainfall in June 2026, with cumulative precipitation expected to reach approximately 700 mm, including about 400 mm during the last two weeks of June, significantly increasing the risk of flooding and landslides. Historical comparison shows that flood impacts vary considerably according to rainfall intensity: while the 2024 floods caused around 20 deaths, 2025 experienced more moderate rainfall with no reported flood-related fatalities. This 2026 event, despite being at the beginning of the highest rainfall weeks, has had a more severe humanitarian impact, resulting in fatalities, injuries, damaged and destroyed homes, displacement, and disruption of essential services, highlighting its exceptional nature compared to recent years.

On 1 July 2026, the Government of Côte d'Ivoire officially acknowledged the severity of the humanitarian situation during the Council of Ministers, highlighting the scale of the impacts caused by the floods and landslides and the urgent need to support affected communities. This official recognition of the emergency constituted the trigger for the Côte d'Ivoire Red Cross (CRCI) to activate its response mechanisms and initiate the preparation of a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) request. Following this activation, CRCI launched rapid needs assessments in the most affected areas to determine the extent of the damage, identify the priority needs of affected households and inform the design of an appropriate humanitarian response.

title: Mali Complex Emergency 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRML022)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
05-06-2026

What happened, where and when?

On the night of April 24 to 25, 2026, Mali was confronted with a series of coordinated armed attacks on a scale not seen since the 2012 rebellion. These attacks were carried out simultaneously by the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and the Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) against several strategic localities in the country.

The attacks mainly targeted military positions and strategic infrastructure. They have also had a direct impact on nearby residential areas, resulting in loss of life, destruction of property and a widespread climate of fear and uncertainty. Population movements have been disrupted, economic activities temporarily slowed down and access to some essential services made more difficult, thus increasing the vulnerability of communities already affected by years of crisis.

In addition, the security situation continues to deteriorate, with numerous reports of blockades of towns and villages by armed groups, burning of public transport vehicles on main roads, abductions of people and destruction of agricultural crops. At the same time, weather forecasts point to a high risk of flooding in several areas of the country, which could further increase humanitarian needs.

The attacks affected several regions of Mali, including:
- District of Bamako;

- Koulikoro region, in particular the city of Kati;
- Mopti region, in particular Sévaré and Bandiagara;
- Gao region;
- Kidal Region;
- as well as certain areas of central Mali.

The attacks took place on the night of April 24 to 25, 2026. However, the situation remains ongoing and highly volatile.

These events are part of a context of continuous deterioration of the security situation observed since 2024, marked in particular by the attack on Bamako airport in September 2024 and by the prolonged disruptions in fuel supply since September 2025.

Following the attacks of 25 April 2026, the Mali Red Cross (RCM), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) conducted a joint analysis of the security context and activated the Movement's coordination mechanisms within the framework of the Seville Agreement 2.0. This analysis indicates a high risk of further deterioration of the situation, with further displacement, increased humanitarian needs and increased difficulties in accessing essential services.

The current context is also marked by the implementation of restrictive measures recently adopted by the authorities, in particular the ban on the circulation and marketing of certain categories of motorcycles in several areas affected by insecurity through an interministerial order dated June 2, 2026. Although these measures are motivated by security imperatives, they have a significant impact on people's livelihoods, as motorcycles are the main means of transporting people, goods and basic services in many localities. Mobility restrictions limit access to markets, health facilities, schools and economic opportunities, leading to a decrease in the incomes of households already weakened by insecurity.

At the same time, restrictions on access to certain forest areas considered sensitive further reduce the livelihoods of communities. Many households depend on forest resources for firewood collection, charcoal production, non-timber forest product gathering, grazing and certain income-generating activities. Limiting these activities increases the economic vulnerability of populations, increases the risk of food insecurity and reduces households' coping mechanisms in the face of successive shocks.

In this context, an inter-headquarters meeting of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement was held on 5 June 2026 between the CRM, the IFRC and the ICRC. This meeting provided an opportunity to carry out an up-to-date joint analysis of the security, humanitarian and operational context as well as to assess the implications of recent developments on the affected populations and on the Movement's response capacities.

The conclusions of this meeting highlighted a continued deterioration of the context, characterized by the geographical spread of insecurity, the multiplication of restrictions on movement, the weakening of household livelihoods, the increased risks of population displacement and the gradual deterioration of access to essential services. The Movement partners also stressed the need to strengthen operational preparedness and coordination mechanisms in order to respond effectively to a possible escalation of the crisis.

The launch of this operation is based on the recommendations and analyses resulting from this inter-headquarters coordination meeting of the Movement held on 5 June 2026, organized within the framework of the coordination mechanisms provided for in the Seville Agreement 2.0. The joint analysis concludes that there is a high risk of further deterioration of the situation in the coming months, with a likely increase in humanitarian needs, additional population displacement and increasing access constraints for humanitarian actors. This is consistent with the findings of the UNHCR assessment of 2 June 2026.

The forward-looking scenarios developed by the Movement anticipate a protracted conflict in the short and medium term, marked by progressive fragmentation of territory, a reduction in the effective presence of the State in certain areas and increased pressure on civilian populations. In this context, the Mali Red Cross is currently operating under Code Orange, with its Emergency Operations Centre(EOC) activated and its Emergency Brigades (BU) mobilised to ensure a rapid response to emerging needs and to strengthen preparedness in the face of a possible deterioration of the situation.

title: Cox's Bazar Monsoon Response 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRBD040)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
05-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since 5th July 2026, Cox’s Bazar District has experienced an intense heavy monsoon rainfall associated with a monsoon depression over the Bay of Bengal. Although the system later weakened into a well-marked low-pressure area inland, active monsoon conditions continued to bring widespread heavy rainfall, rough sea conditions, and localized severe weather impacts across the district. As of 12 July 1800 hours BST, Cox’s Bazar had experienced a cumulative rainfall of 810 mm since 5th July, recorded as the highest continuous rainfall volume for monsoon season in Cox's Bazar compared to the previous years.

The prolonged rainfall has caused significant humanitarian impacts across both the 33 Rohingya camps and host communities in Cox’s Bazar district. In the camps, heavy rainfall and saturated slopes triggered landslides, flooding, wind-related damage, and infrastructure disruptions, damaging shelters, WASH facilities, access routes, pathways, retaining walls, and essential service points.

The impact has also extended to adjacent host communities, where heavy rainfall worsened flooding to at least 49% of Cox's Bazar district's administrative jurisdiction particularly in Chakariya, Pekua, and Matamuhuri sub-districts, disrupting mobility, communication, livelihoods, and access to basic services along damaged shelters, critical infrastructures, and services.

In response to the escalating situation, Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) activated its Population Movement Operation (PMO) Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and mobilized staff and volunteers to support early warning dissemination, emergency relocation, incident monitoring, damage assessment, search and rescue support, and immediate assistance to affected households using available contingency resources. BDRCS has also continued coordination with camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs), local authorities, Cyclone Preparedness Programme (CPP), Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), the Rohingya Coordination Platform (RCP)-Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) Working Group, Site Management, and relevant sector actors. However, with continued rainfall forecast and ground conditions already saturated, the risk of further flooding, landslides, displacement, damage to shelters and services, and depletion of existing response capacity remains high.

title: MAR: Fire - 07-2026 - Ouneine-Ijoukak Wildfire (2026-07-17)
content:
Description

On Wednesday, July 15, a wildfire has broken out in the forest area located between the mountainous communes of Ounaine, in Taroudant Province, and Ijoukak, in Al Haouz province, west-central and southwestern Morocco. The fire spread rapidly due to a combination of strong winds, high temperatures, and rugged mountainous terrain, increasing the risk to surrounding forest ecosystems and nearby communities. Early estimates indicated an affected area of 100 hectares.

Emergency response operations were swiftly launched to contain the blaze. Access to the affected area is challenging because of the steep and difficult terrain, limiting the deployment of heavy firefighting equipment and complicating suppression efforts. Intervention focused on preventing the fire from reaching nearby inhabited areas through manual extinction and aerial firefighting. According to the latest official statements, 14 hectares have been consumed by the fires in Al Haouz. Authorities in Taroudant are yet to release corresponding figures.

While the fire is reportedly contained on the Ijoukak side with no deaths or injuries, authorities remain vigilant. MRCS continues to assess the situation in coordination with the local actors.

title: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Heavy rainfall, Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #2 (2026-07-19)
content:
Description

Heavy rainfall from 15–17 July triggered flash floods and landslides across Lai Chau Province, with Muong Than Commune being the worst affected. In response to the severity of the disaster, the Lai Chau Provincial People's Committee declared a state of disaster emergency for Muong Than on 17 July (Decision No. 1501/QĐ-UBND).

Initial reports indicate that flash floods destroyed and buried houses in several villages, including Doi 9, Doi 11, Sap Ngua, Che Bo and Chit. National Highways 32 and 279, together with several local roads, have been cut off by landslides, significantly disrupting access and emergency response. Casualty figures continue to be updated as search and rescue operations progress. As of the morning of 18 July, authorities reported at least four fatalities, four people missing and seven injured, while approximately 80 households (358 people) have been evacuated from high-risk areas.

According to the initial rapid reports from Lao Cai, Lai Chau, Dien Bien and Son La provinces, heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides occurring between 15 and 17 July 2026 caused the following impacts:

  • Human impact: Four person was killed, four people remain missing/unaccounted for, and seven people were injured (all in Lai Chau Province).
  • Housing: A total of 20 houses were destroyed (17 in Lai Chau and 3 in Son La); 113 houses were damaged (88 in Lao Cai, 2 in Lai Chau, 13 in Dien Bien and 10 in Son La); 42 households were urgently evacuated (26 in Lai Chau and 16 in Son La); and 46 houses were affected by flooding and landslides (29 in Lai Chau and 17 in Dien Bien).
  • Agriculture: Approximately 238.82 hectares of rice and other crops were damaged, including 65.51 ha in Lao Cai, 101.44 ha in Lai Chau, 31.67 ha in Dien Bien, and 40.2 ha in Son La.
  • Livestock: 25 livestock animals and 45 poultry were lost.
  • Transport: Multiple landslides caused significant disruption to transportation. In Lai Chau, several sections of National Highways 4H, 12, 32 and 279, as well as Provincial Roads 127, 128, 129, 133, 133B, 134 and 135, were blocked. In Son La, 32 landslide sites were recorded along Provincial Road 109. In Dien Bien, disruptions occurred on National Highways 12 and 279 and Provincial Road 143, while numerous commune and village roads across the affected provinces were also blocked.
  • Power supply: In Lai Chau Province, approximately 1,373 electricity customers remained without power.

Total estimated losses to housing, crops, vegetation, roads and power lines amount to more than VNĐ120 billion (US$4.6 million).

The Viet Nam Red Cross (VNRC) has mobilized its provincial chapter, district branches and volunteers to support the ongoing emergency response in Lai Chau Province. In coordination with local authorities, Red Cross volunteers are providing logistical support by preparing and delivering food, drinking water and refreshments for military personnel and emergency responders conducting search and rescue operations. Simultaneously, the VNRC is carrying out rapid assessments of humanitarian needs and maintaining close coordination with local authorities to determine appropriate assistance for affected communities as the situation evolves.

The IFRC continues to monitor the evolving situation in close coordination with the VNRC and stands ready to provide technical and operational support should humanitarian needs increase or additional assistance be required.

Actions taken by others

Immediately after the disaster, local forces in Mường Than Commune mobilised for rescue operations. Leadership of the Lai Châu Provincial People's Committee formed a working delegation to go directly to the scene and take command of search and rescue efforts. Provincial police and military units were deployed with equipment and support vehicles to focus on disaster relief, search and rescue operations. Lai Châu Provincial Police established a forward command post at Tân Uyên Commune Police station, under the direct command of Colonel Khoàng Văn Thương, Deputy Director of the Provincial Police, to co-ordinate rescue, relief and disaster recovery operations. The Chairman of the Lai Châu Provincial People's Committee issued an urgent directive on July 17, instructing departments, agencies, armed forces and local People's Committees to focus on responding to and recovering from the floods, flash floods and landslides in accordance with the "four on-the-spot" principle, with no room for passivity or unpreparedness. Emergency declarations have been issued for Mường Than Commune and for a landslide site that has severed National Highway 12 within Lê Lợi Commune. Rescue operations in Mường Than Commune are proceeding with urgency. Provincial People's Committee chairman travelled to the scene to inspect and direct recovery efforts and oversee disaster response measures. Provincial and local forces are deploying personnel and equipment to search and rescue operations and disaster relief work, with the aim of restoring stability to residents' lives as quickly as possible.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide (2026-07-19)
content:
Description

Bangladesh has experienced widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across its south-eastern and north-eastern regions following several days of exceptionally heavy monsoon rainfall. The emergency was initially triggered by a low-pressure system that brought intense rainfall across large parts of the country, resulting in severe flooding, waterlogging, river overflows, and landslides in vulnerable areas. Rainfall totals were particularly high in Chattogram, Teknaf, Bandarban, and Sylhet districts. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm of rainfall on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf received 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm), and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm).

Although weather conditions have gradually improved, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecasts that active monsoon conditions will continue through 20 July, bringing light to moderate rainfall accompanied by temporary gusty winds across the country. Maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla, and Payra remain under Local Cautionary Signal No. 3. Hydrological conditions have improved significantly since the peak of the emergency. As of 16 July, only the Kushiyara River remained above the danger level at two monitoring stations, Markuli in Sunamganj and Fenchuganj in Sylhet. Water levels along the Surma River and other major rivers in the north-eastern region have continued to recede, and flood conditions in low-lying areas of Sylhet and Sunamganj are expected to improve further. Similarly, water levels in the Teesta, Dharla, and Dudhkumar rivers in Rangpur Division have fallen and are projected to continue decreasing. Nevertheless, localized flooding, waterlogging, and landslide risks persist in several areas where saturated soils, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to affect communities. The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) Emergency Operations Centre remains active and continues to monitor the evolving situation.

At the peak of the emergency, flood conditions deteriorated rapidly. Several rivers, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu, and Khowai, exceeded danger levels, with the Sangu River in Bandarban rising more than two metres above its danger threshold. Rising river levels threatened low-lying communities in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh, and the northern river basins, causing widespread disruption to livelihoods, infrastructure, transportation networks, and basic services.

The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,116,174 people have been affected across 10 districts. The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people were temporarily displaced, while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters were opened to accommodate affected populations. Government reporting further indicates that 267,918 households were stranded or isolated by floodwaters across seven districts. Media reports citing MoDMR indicate that at least 59 people lost their lives nationwide as a result of floods and landslides.

Housing damage has been extensive across the affected areas. Preliminary government assessments indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban, 13,860 in Chattogram, 1,040 in Khagrachhari, 1,613 in Cox’s Bazar. However, the full extent of housing damage remains unclear as standing water, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to hamper detailed assessments. According to the MoDMR situation update on 18 July 2026, a total of 374 unions and four municipalities across 56 upazilas have been affected by the ongoing floods.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems have been severely disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts. In many areas, water supply infrastructure remains submerged, damaged, or contaminated by floodwaters carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste, and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 water points had been fully or partially damaged, increasing risks of waterborne disease outbreaks and reducing access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities.

The floods have also caused substantial damage to agriculture, livestock, and fisheries, threatening household incomes, food security, and rural livelihoods. According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), approximately 54,470 hectares of cropland and 324,358 farming households have been affected by heavy rainfall and associated hazards. Crop losses alone are estimated at more than 54,409 hectares of agricultural land. The fisheries sector has sustained particularly severe damage, with preliminary assessments from the Department of Fisheries (DoF) indicating losses of 7,613 metric tons of fish and prawns. Floodwaters washed away 21,764 fishponds and 784 commercial enclosures covering 8,966 hectares, resulting in estimated losses of approximately USD 18.3 million.

The livestock sector has also been heavily impacted. Approximately 266,038 cattle and buffalo, 173,592 goats and sheep, 2.85 million chickens, and 62,811 ducks have been affected. Reported animal deaths include 62 cattle, 139 goats, 59 sheep, 154,528 chickens, and 2,063 ducks. Total losses in the livestock sector are estimated at BDT 576.2 million (approximately USD 4.7 million). Combined losses across the fisheries and livestock sectors are estimated at approximately USD 23 million.

The most severely affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj, where communities continue to face challenges related to damaged housing, disrupted livelihoods, limited access to essential services, and deteriorated infrastructure.

In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and surrounding host communities. Across the 33 refugee camps, flooding and landslides affected more than 28,000 people, damaged over 3,100 shelters, and displaced more than 4,700 individuals. Multiple casualties and injuries were reported as a result of landslides and flood-related incidents. UNHCR has confirmed 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees, while thousands of people have been left homeless following landslides and shelter collapses, further increasing humanitarian needs among already vulnerable populations.

The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has maintained a coordinated multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected communities. Response measures have included the opening of more than 1,000 evacuation shelters, the distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water, and other relief items, as well as the deployment of the Bangladesh Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and Civil Defence, and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation, and relief operations. The Government has also mobilised 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas to address urgent health needs and reduce public health risks. In addition, the Government has allocated 3,350 metric tons of rice, BDT 23.5 million in cash assistance, and 4,200 bundles of corrugated galvanized iron (CGI) sheets alongside BDT 12.6 million for shelter repair and reconstruction support for affected households across seven districts. National and district-level coordination mechanisms remain active to monitor the evolving situation, facilitate early warning dissemination, support affected communities, and prioritize assistance to the hardest-hit areas. Efforts are ongoing to restore essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian and early recovery needs as floodwaters continue to recede.

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

No
